title: 4Sum II
statement: Given four integer arrays a, b, c and d, each of length n, count the index tuples (i, j, k, l) for which a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] == 0. The four indices are chosen independently — one from each array — so tuples that pick equal values at different indices are counted separately.
realWorld: Joining four independent dimensions on a sum constraint is the shape of a multi-way join with a computed predicate, and a query planner faced with it does exactly this: rather than a four-way nested loop, it builds a hash table on the aggregate of two relations and probes it with the aggregate of the other two. The technique is also the standard attack on subset-sum-style problems in cryptanalysis, where halving the exponent is the difference between feasible and not.

examples.explanation: One tuple, and a useful trap: because the sum is 0, looking up a[i]+b[j] instead of its negation still gives the right answer here.

Two pairs from a and b sum to 0 — (1,-1) and (2,-2) — and each combines with all four (k,l) pairs from c and d. The multiplicities are the whole answer, which is why the table must store counts rather than mere presence.

constraints: The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer

bruteForce.idea: Four nested loops over the four arrays, incrementing a counter whenever the four values sum to zero.
bruteForce.whySlow: The two inner loops exist only to ask 'how many pairs from c and d sum to -(x + y)?', and they rebuild the complete table of c+d sums from scratch for every one of the n^2 outer pairs. That table never changes — it depends on c and d alone — yet it is re-derived n^2 times and discarded each time. At n = 200 that is 1.6 * 10^9 additions to compute a 40,000-entry table 40,000 times over.

patternIdentification: A constraint spanning four independent choices can be split down the middle: a + b == -(c + d). Each half has only n^2 combinations, so tabulate one half's sums with their multiplicities, then walk the other half and look up each complement. Meet in the middle turns a product of k loops into two products of k/2, and hashing is what makes the join free. The precondition to check before reaching for it — and the reason this works here — is that the two halves are *independent*: any pair from a and b may be combined with any pair from c and d, because the four arrays are separate and no element can be reused across halves. That is exactly what the ordinary 4Sum problem (one array, four distinct indices) lacks: there a left pair and a right pair can share an index, so a plain multiplicity table would count quadruplets that use the same element twice, and repairing that means carrying index sets rather than counts — at which point the tabulation buys nothing. Whenever you split a constraint in half, the question to ask is whether the halves can collide.

optimized.idea: Build a map from every a[i] + b[j] to the number of (i, j) pairs producing it — n^2 insertions. Then iterate every (k, l) pair from c and d and add the map's count for -(c[k] + d[l]); each stored pair is a genuinely distinct tuple, so the counts multiply out correctly without any per-tuple enumeration. Storing counts rather than presence is not an optimisation but a correctness requirement: four different (i, j) pairs that all sum to 0 represent four different tuples for every matching (k, l).

commonMistakes: Storing presence in a Set instead of multiplicities in a Map — a = [1,1], b = [-1,-1], c = [0,0], d = [0,0] returns 4 instead of 16, because the four distinct (i, j) pairs that all sum to 0 collapse into a single key and each probe adds 1 rather than 4.

Probing with `sums.get(z + w)` instead of `sums.get(-(z + w))` — the missing negation counts tuples whose halves are equal rather than opposite. The all-zeros example still returns 1, so the smallest test passes while every input with non-zero values is wrong.

Reusing this template for the single-array 4Sum with four distinct indices — the pair table cannot tell whether a left pair and a right pair share an index, so nums = [0,0,0,0] with target 0 reports 16 quadruplets where only one exists. The split is only sound when the halves draw from disjoint sources.
